quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
quiz_item.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.
choices: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Warm water restores flexibility to dried reed and wood splints so they weave smoothly without splintering, and sharp basketry shears, knives, and awls must always be directed away from fingers and the body.

pamphlet_excerpts: Common Basketry Weave Patterns: The following are common weaves used in this pamphlet (p. 11).
Over-Under Plain Weave Structure: Sometimes called over-under weave, the plain weave is done with rigid stakes or spokes, and weavers that wrap around the stakes in an over-one (p. 11).
Rigid Stakes Versus Weavers: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reed than weavers (p. 11).
Continuous Weave Visual Similarity: Continuous weave looks much the same as plain weave, but it is woven with a different technique (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Rigid Structural Spokes: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reed than weavers (p. 11).
Step 2 - Distinguish Continuous Weave Method: Continuous weave looks much the same as plain weave, but it is woven with a different technique (p. 11).
Step 3 - Set Up Odd Stakes: This weave is created over an odd number of stakes (p. 11).
Step 4 - Weave Continuously Adding Reed: It is not done one row at a time, but continuously from beginning to end, with additional weavers added when more length is needed (p. 11).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does a continuous weave differ in construction from a standard row-by-row plain weave?
quiz_item.question: How does a continuous weave differ in construction from a standard row-by-row plain weave?
options: A. It is woven over an even number of flat wooden slats without any spokes.
B. It uses weavers that are much thicker and stiffer than the upright stakes.
C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
D. It requires sewing coiled pine needles together with waxed thread.
choices: A. It is woven over an even number of flat wooden slats without any spokes.
B. It uses weavers that are much thicker and stiffer than the upright stakes.
C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
D. It requires sewing coiled pine needles together with waxed thread.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Continuous weave looks like plain weave, but it is created over an odd number of stakes and woven continuously from start to finish rather than one row at a time (p. 11).

common_misconception_pair.misconception: Pulling weavers as tightly as possible around the corners of a square basket is the best way to create ninety-degree angles.
common_misconception_pair.fact: Pulling weavers too tightly bows the corner stakes inward and turns a square basket into a round one; instead, gently pinch and shape each corner without over-tightening (p. 18).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.
choices: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Warm water restores flexibility to dried reed and wood splints so they weave smoothly without splintering, and sharp basketry shears, knives, and awls must always be directed away from fingers and the body.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a continuous weave differ in construction from a standard row-by-row plain weave?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a continuous weave differ in construction from a standard row-by-row plain weave?
options: A. It is woven over an even number of flat wooden slats without any spokes.
B. It uses weavers that are much thicker and stiffer than the upright stakes.
C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
D. It requires sewing coiled pine needles together with waxed thread.
choices: A. It is woven over an even number of flat wooden slats without any spokes.
B. It uses weavers that are much thicker and stiffer than the upright stakes.
C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
D. It requires sewing coiled pine needles together with waxed thread.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It is woven over an odd number of stakes from beginning to end rather than one separate row at a time.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Continuous weave looks like plain weave, but it is created over an odd number of stakes and woven continuously from start to finish rather than one row at a time (p. 11).
